items.title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
items.author: ambewas
items.content:
I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors.

I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created.

Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),…

Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027.

Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today.

You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.)

The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve.

I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine.

Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend.

Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT.

What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily?

I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

items.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
items.author: brownrout
items.content:
Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.

Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.

As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.

I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.

To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).

I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use.

Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

items.title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
items.author: paulirish
items.content:
+JS based pattern. We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge.

200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves. (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1]

I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU.

We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.)

People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :) We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided.

    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal"
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src
If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler!

An isometric pixel-art map of València, in the spirit of SimCity and of Isometric NYC. Every building is a real one, drawn from above at the same angle, block by block.

The whole municipal term is painted, from the huerta to the Albufera, except a few small huerta exclaves where there's no 3D imagery to paint from.

items.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
items.author: shayan_abbas
items.content:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).

For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.

DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.

                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark.

It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch: Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am) Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable Organization of connections into projects

Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.

Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.

The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.

Limitations: It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon. Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.

Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.

items.title: Show HN: Micron – Oberon with the Power of C
items.author: Rochus
items.content:
I have been developing Micron (for "MicroOberon"), a lean, statically typed, modular systems programming language that combines Oberon’s simplicity and explicit module structure with C’s low-level capabilities and interoperability.

Micron is not my first langage design. I first built Oberon+, a modernized and unified Oberon, in order to under­ stand, by implementing it and by porting real systems to it, what Wirth’s design actually gives and where it fails. The systems ported to Oberon+ included the 2013 Project Oberon System and different versions of Oberon System 3. I then explored the opposite direction with Luon, a higher-level language for managed application progamming. Micron is the synthesis of this and my 30 years experience with C/C++ in systems programming.

The goal of Micron is to use the same language for boot code, device drivers, an operating system kernel, and ordinary applications, without requiring a garbage collector or routing machine access through a separate, unchecked system dialect (such as Oberon's SYSTEM.ADR/GET/PUT which operates on LONGINT). The language supports explicit memory layouts, signed and unsigned integer types, pointer operations, and direct calls to C without wrappers. One of its central design choices is language levels. Each module declars the level and thus the feature it needs, ranging from code that requires neither stack nor heap to garbage-collected objects. A module can import only modules at the same or a lower level. For example, a kernel module declared at level 1 cannot accidentally acquire a dependency on heap allocation through an import. Other features include generic modules, structural interfaces, and compile-time procedures. Much of what would require a preprocessor in C is expressed through typed language features.

There is a working compiler, interpreter, and IDE, along with a free textbook (http://software.rochus-keller.ch/micron-textbook.pdf). The book explains both how the language works and the reasons behind its design. Its systems-programming section walks through a port of Wirth and Gutknecht’s Project Oberon operating system to Micron, cross-compiled and linked into a single executabl that runs on an emulated RISC-V machine.

The examples also include ports of a Smalltalk-80 VM, Scheme 9, and the original P4 Pascal compiler. The compiler and interpreter implement the language specification; native backends and tooling are still work in progress, and the current native code generation prioritises simplicity over optimisation.

items.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
items.author: hedgerow-dev
items.content:
I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake.

To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers.

Things that were fun to get right:

- Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes.

- Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities.

- Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real.

Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io.

Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!

items.title: Show HN: Waymark – A workflow engine that compiles jobs instead of replaying
items.author: icyfox
items.content:
Hey everyone! @mozgiii and I have been working on Waymark for the better part of the last year. Waymark’s an open source durable execution library with similar functionality to Temporal or DBOS.

I fell in love with durable execution a few years ago, after working at a company with a heavy pubsub architecture. In comparison to job orchestrators that force a certain task design or special syntax, many of these durable libs lets you write business logic in regular code: `asyncio.gather` to parallelize tasks, `for` loops, conditionals, and let the runtime figure out how to run them efficiently across a cluster of nodes. But most of the current solutions require a heavy broker, runtime hacks to try to ensure deterministic workflow logic, and feel like you have to learn a whole new ecosystem just to get started.

A few unique design decisions in waymark:

— Write jobs in normal code (right now Python but JS coming soon). Instead of running control flow as-is, which requires booting up an interpreter to replay past state, we’ll just compile your code directly. We walk your AST and map your logic to our stackless VM bytecode. We support variables, conditionals, await, sleep, helper functions, loops... basically what you’d expect in workflow logic.

— Since we’re compiling a language subset, we can proactively flag errors in your workflows locally instead of when they run in production.

— It only requires Postgres as the task broker. We’ve spent a lot of time tuning our design to play nicely with its strengths and limitations; our current benchmarks show around 1500 workflows/second but we still have some more optimization work to do here.

— Actions plug-and-play with FastAPI’s dependency injection syntax. So if you already have an ecosystem based on typehinting/DI, it should fit like a glove.

It allows for parallelization of workflows across one machine or a whole cluster. The bulk of the work per node is done by our central Rust core - which distributes workflows to properly saturate all cores. The idea is to be as batteries included as possible with the broker, webapp, and runtime.

What to use it for? It works great as the runner loop controlling agents, but it also works well for basically any task that you need to kick off in the background. It’s largely replaced our way of writing api code. Most frontend actions at this point just push to a simple REST endpoint that kick off a background job.

I spent an embarrassing amount of time making our https://waymark.sh site interactive - it’s probably the best place to learn more. We’re starting with Python support and looking for community input on what language to ship next. Would love to hear your thoughts!

items.title: Show HN: Spindle – a full-featured, type-safe web framework for OCaml 5
items.author: zaiev
items.content:
Spindle is a multicore-by-design, eio-native web framework for modern OCaml.

Its central idea is to provide an expressive, type-driven API and derive the rest: codecs, request validation, OpenAPI spec and frontend schemas (Zod and Melange). This keeps contracts in sync between server and client without maintaining separate definitions.

The framework includes an RFC-strict HTTP server, composable dependencies, WebSockets, SSE and high-level primitives for building MCP servers. It also provides production-ready essentials like distributed tracing, OT-compatible metrics, logging and other features you would expect. Speed was never the goal but the benchmarks show it running x2 faster than NestJS and x5 faster than FastAPI on a single core.

items.title: Show HN: A decent text-to-image model trained for ~$20K (Apache 2.0 Weights)
items.author: schopra909
items.content:
Pressure testing the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT)

For us, this $21K training run is a proof-of-concept along the way to our next video model. We were surprised by how good the results looked given the size of the model, so we thought we'd share it with the world as an experimental release.

If you haven't followed our work previously, we'd love to take a step back and introduce ourselves. We're a 2-person research lab training our own generative video models entirely from scratch. The ultimate ambition is creative tools that democratize access to animation. You can read more about that .

Today, generative video models have two major flaws: they are too slow/expensive and they lack proper controls. Creativity is an iterative process. You make, you tweak, you get better. With this double whammy, video models (as they stand today) are effectively useless for storytelling.

When we set out to build Linum v3 earlier this year, the primary goal was to bring the cost envelope of inference down significantly. If our model is fast and cheap, it's the first step (of many) towards useful creative tools.

We've written extensively about the steps we've taken in this direction, but here's the long story short:

  • The bottleneck for training and inference for video is attention, O(n²). If we can compress more aggressively, we'll reduce the context window for attention, slashing the cost of training and inference.
  • Typically, compression is handled by a separate specialized model like a Variational Autoencoder, but that's not necessarily optimal. VAEs seem to have an empirical on the amount of compression they can achieve. More importantly, improving the VAE on its task of reconstruction can produce worse in the downstream diffusion model.
  • If you get rid of the VAE altogether, you should be able to compress more aggressively and learn faster. Diffusion models are a more powerful family of generative models than VAEs. We should be able to use them to compress and generate at the same time. Instead of using another model's latent space, the diffusion model should learn a latent space purpose-built for its use case. In turn, we should be able to squeeze more juice out of this compression.

In our last blog, we iterated towards a new architecture that we called the Pyramid-JiT (P-JiT). It's a pixel-space model that converges in 11× fewer samples than Linum v2 with 4× more aggressive token reduction (i.e., we represent a 512² image in the same number of tokens we used to represent a 256² image).

For the details on how we got there, we'd recommend you take a look at our previous blogs on and . But at a high level, we found a noise schedule for pixel-space models that helps the models better learn fine-grained detail. And, we added readouts along the trunk of the DiT.

Adjacent work in , , and all point to weak gradients in the early blocks of the DiT. By operating in pixel space, every block of our DiT is quite literally predicting a version of the final image, so we can boost gradient signal earlier in the network by predicting low-resolution versions of the final image. This helps accelerate convergence.

The architecture did well in our initial experiments, but we wanted to see how it performed when we trained it for longer (i.e., ~600M samples instead of 50–100M samples). It's a pressure test of sorts along the way towards larger models (and video).

Text and image each pass through two single-modality "refiner" DiT blocks, then merge into one stream of 22 identical DiT blocks. The text representation comes from a frozen Qwen3.5-4B model, which we read at layers 7, 15 and 27 (its three full-attention layers). We concatenate and project these representations into the text refiner. The image is split into 32×32 patches and compressed into a 1024-dimensional space, before being projected up into the image refiner blocks.

At block 5, we have a 2-layer readout that aligns the model's latent space to DINOv3-L. We have two linear readout heads along the trunk after blocks 10 and 16. As discussed earlier, these predict the clean image at a quarter and half resolution, respectively. The total loss is given by MSE at the readouts, PixelREPA cosine-distance, MSE at the final output head, and perceptual losses on the full resolution image ( and ).

Every DiT block is conditioned on the timestep through a low-rank AdaLN, following . The timestep embedding goes through one down-projection to 256-dim. Each block then has its own up-projection to a scale and a gate, zero-initialized so every block starts as the identity.

As described in our last blog, we employ a curriculum over the noise schedule. We start concentrated at high noise for the first 80M samples, so the model learns basic structure. Then, we widen the noise distribution for the remaining training time so it can learn fine-grained details. See Appendix A for details.

We start EMA at 100M samples, so the model has already learned decent representations of structure and detail. When we switch to 1024², we start with a fresh optimizer and resume training from the 512² EMA weights. At 1024² we double the noise scale from 2 to 4 to account for the redundancy of information (see JiT, Appendix ). The higher noise level and need to reproduce fine detail exactly at high resolution result in a higher overall loss, even as image quality improves rapidly. We use RoPE interpolation in the resolution transition. Moreover, we start the 1024² EMA 2M samples in, so it has adjusted to the new resolution before we start the averaging process.

It's still early days for post-training diffusion models

To be blunt, post-training is a very young discipline within diffusion models, and we've only seen the first sparks of it working in the past few months.

Of course there's been a lot of work in model and schedule distillation, but when it comes to post-training in terms of improving fundamental model capabilities (like we've seen with coding in LLMs over the past 18 months), it hasn't really come to fruition just yet for diffusion.

DPO has been around for a while, but tends to dramatically overfit to specific aesthetic choices. was one of the first articulations of bringing RLVR-style frameworks to diffusion, and that only came out last fall. Since then there have been a few papers like Diffusion and this June's (the best articulation of diffusion post-training so far, in our opinion).

We think that this difficulty in adapting techniques comes down to the fact that we don't have access to strong likelihood estimates in diffusion models like we have in auto-regressive LLMs. We'll dive more into these concerns and our full post-training stack in the coming weeks.

This model was not trained with images of rendered text (no infographics, PDFs, pages of books, PowerPoint slides), so it cannot write text or generate posters. As we detailed in our data filtration , we don't consider this data useful for our ultimate goal of animation tools, so this text-heavy data has been filtered out entirely from our dataset.

This is a small model (2B-parameter DiT, 4B text encoder), and accordingly there are a few areas where the model struggles: full body, many entities (e.g. 6 cars, crowds), multi-person interactions, and world knowledge. The model is capable of correctly generating these images on occasion. Training a larger model (e.g. 7B parameters) and further post-training would likely mitigate these issues.

items.title: Show HN: Vegetable Gardening for Engineers
items.author: jrcplus
items.content:
This is a starting point for understanding how to grow vegetables at home. I created this document out of dissatisfaction with popular gardening books (too little detail) and social media (too much talking and clickbait). I found myself organizing and synthesizing concepts, data, and advice from disparate sources. I even turned to material from agricultural university extension programs, crop guides from commercial seed and fertilizer companies, high school biology courses, live farmer training courses and gardening workshops, and techniques from indoor cannabis growers.

This document reflects my personal learning journey over the past years. You are welcome to submit pull requests or email me with feedback.

Currently the focus is on indoor and balcony growing in an urban apartment setting. Therefore, only hydroponics and container gardening are covered. Garden beds, composting, aquaculture, fungiculture, permaculture are not covered (yet).

This document is organized broadly in three parts:

The first part provides a conceptual understanding of the science of growing vegetables. The second part features tables of data (“VegTable”) for many garden crops. It answers basic questions about crop selection. The third part is a collection of links about well-known growing systems, techniques, and other resources. Finally, the last part examines the economics of market gardening.

☯️ Environmental parameters

When growing plants, your task is to balance a number of highly interdependent factors, as listed below. An insufficient amount of, say, light or nutrition creates a limiting factor in plant growth and development. On the other hand, excessive light or fertilizer (i.e. beyond what a specific plant species can handle at a given metabolic rate) can also result in problems (tip burn, photo-oxidative stress).

* key measurements for small-scale systems

Why are these relevant? Plants perform two critical processes which are complementary:

  • Plants convert light energy into storable chemical energy (carbohydrates) during . In other words: ☀️ Light energy + 💨 Carbon dioxide + 💧 Water → 🔋 Stored energy + 💨 Oxygen
  • Plants use the stored energy (carbohydrates) to fuel growth, in a process called . In other words: 🔋 Stored energy + 💨 Oxygen → 💨 Carbon dioxide + 💧 Water

is the single most important environmental parameter as it literally provides energy for plant growth.

dictates a plant’s metabolic rate and therefore also strongly influences growth rate.

Additionally, there is another critical process:

  • The evaporation of water through a plant’s leaves pulls water (containing dissolved nutrients) up from the roots. This is a passive process called .

is sometimes called a “master variable” as it affects the solubility of soil nutrients (among other things, including microbial activity) and therefore nutrient availability, hence plant growth.

Air , , and all affect the rate of transpiration and also therefore nutrient uptake and plant growth. For this reason, poor ventilation actually can result in nutrient deficiencies.

On the other hand, excessive ventilation decreases relative humidity which, in combination with heating the cooler incoming air (air holds more water at warmer temperatures), can increase transpiration, which decreases plant temperature and increases ambient humidity, resulting in a vicious cycle. Alternatively, if transpiration occurs to the extent that there is not enough water in the plant (e.g. during peak hours of the day), then stomata (microscopic openings on the undersides of leaves) will close, which increases leaf temperatures and decreases CO₂ exchange… [1]

Humidity can be reduced in three ways: 1) heating (air holds more water at warmer temperatures), 2) ventilation (“out”), and 3) condensation (“in”).

  • In an indoor system, the environmental parameters are mostly controlled. Limiting factors are likely 1) light, 2) space (area), 3) water, 4) nutrition, 5) oxygen (for soil-less systems and compact soils).
  • In an outdoor system, think about sun, wind, temperature, water access, soil conditions. Look for planting calendars and first/last frost dates.
  • Mary M. Pratt, Practical Science for Gardeners, 2005.
  • Khan Academy, “Cellular respiration”, https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/cellular-respiration-and-fermentation
  • Khan Academy, “Photosynthesis”, https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/photosynthesis-in-plants
  • [1] https://www.greenhousecanada.com/empower-plants-through-balanced-climate-control-33115/
Sowing to radicle (root) emergence
“Sprout”: Radicle emergence to expansion of cotyledons (false leaves)
“Seedling”: Cotyledon expansion to vegetative growth
Growth of all true leaves
From first flowering to first fruit set
From first fruit set to growth, ripening, and first harvest
From first harvest to the end of last harvest

A general rule of thumb is to plant seeds twice as deep as they are large.

  • Mary M. Pratt, Practical Science for Gardeners, 2005.
  • “Chapter 10: Growth, Development, Transpiration, and Translocation as Affected by Abiotic Environmental Factors”, Plant Factory: An Indoor Vertical Farming System for Efficient Quality Food, edited by Toyoki Kozai, Genhua Niu, Michiko Takagaki

refers to the distribution of wavelengths (colors) in a light. The part of the light spectrum most relevant to photosynthesis is 400–700 nm. This range is named Photosynthetically Active Radiation (PAR).

Simplistically speaking, blue light is needed to produce healthy stems and leaves. Red light is needed for flowering and fruiting, as well as seed germination, root growth, and seed production.

Historically it was believed that plants only used PAR light. It is now understood that far-red and ultraviolet light, which are both outside PAR, can affect plant development. Specifically, far-red (FR) light, which penetrates leaves, can tell plants that they are under a canopy and promote growth, whereas blue-violet and ultraviolet light, which are abundant in the sky, can inhibit growth.

  • Color temperature, measured in Kelvin (K), is only relevant to humans, not plants.
  • Buy a full-spectrum light, not a red-blue (“blurple”) light. Although there is research on the effects of changing light quality during growth, in general it is sufficient to use the same constant full-spectrum light from start to finish.

The rate of plant growth scales to (intensity). However, below a certain quantity (the ), there is not enough energy to fuel growth. On the other side, above a certain quantity (the ), plants become damaged. Tolerance levels vary from crop to crop (see the Data section).

Photosynthetic Photon Flux (PPF)The amount of PAR (400–700 nm light) emitted from a source per second.
Photosynthetic Photon Flux Density (PPFD)The amount of PAR that reaches a destination per second.
Daily Light Integral (DLI)The amount of PAR that cumulatively reaches a destination in one day.

PPFD and DLI are spot measurements. They are always relative to a specific distance from the light source.

To calculate DLI, multiply × (“photoperiod”) × 1/1000000 mol/μmol × 3600 sec/hour.

  • Lumens, lux, and foot-candles are only relevant to humans, not plants.
  • Ask for PPFD maps, which show PPFD measurements at various points across a surface for a given lamp height. As an example, the IKEA VÄXER E27 10W grow bulb is capable of producing >250 PPFD over a 6.5 cm radius area at 30 cm height. If you run it for 16 hours/day, the DLI is 14.4 mol/m²/day (see above calculation). This is sufficient for lettuce, which requires 14–17 DLI, but not tomatoes, which require 22–30 DLI.
  • Plant DLI requirements are for total light, including sunlight, so you may be able to provide less supplemental light.
  • A quantum meter is used to measure PPFD. Apps such as Korona (iOS) can be used as low-cost alternatives. See also MIGRO, “Android Smartphone PAR meter hack”, September 25, 2019, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AjkEJjlzGv8.

Photoperiodism refers to how the light cycle affects plant growth and flowering. (e.g. lettuce) only flower when days are shorter than a certain length, (e.g. mung beans) only flower when days are longer than a certain length, and (e.g. tomatoes) flower based on other conditions.

More about plant lighting

  • “Chapter 7: Light”, Plant Factory: An Indoor Vertical Farming System for Efficient Quality Food, edited by Toyoki Kozai, Genhua Niu, Michiko Takagaki
  • AlboPepper, “PAR Light Quality LEDs & HID: Plant Grow Light Basics -101 (pt 1)”, August 17, 2017, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O3dxjk_E2Ac
  • Bruce Bugbee, “PAR, PPF, PPFD, and PFD Explained”, June 27, 2019, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UZO8Fb0ryW8
  • Bruce Bugbee, “Cannabis Grow Lighting Myths and FAQs with Dr. Bruce Bugbee”, Jan 9, 2020, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ID9rE5JewVg
  • Ledtonic, “DLI (Daily Light Integral) Chart - Understand your plants’ PPFD & photoperiod requirements”, May 28, 2019, https://www.ledtonic.com/blogs/guides/dli-daily-light-integral-chart-understand-your-plants-ppfd-photoperiod-requirements
  • Fluence By OSRAM, https://fluence.science/science-articles/
  • Khan Academy, “Plant responses to light”, https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/plant-biology#plant-responses-to-light-cues
  • The Urban Vertical Farming Project, “LEDs For Vertical Farming: Buying Guide For Lights”, June 13, 2017, https://urbanverticalfarmingproject.com/2017/06/13/led-light-buying-guide-for-vertical-farming/

Every plant has a base (minimum) temperature (), an optimal temperature (), and an maximum temperature (). These temperature ranges can vary across growth stages.

Crucially, there is a tradeoff between growth rate and growth quality. Higher temperatures can result in faster growth but also thinner stems, weaker roots, and less flavor. Furthermore, gases become less soluable at higher temperatures, increasing the risk of oxygen deficiency.

Key air temperature measurements are as follows:

Higher DIF can result in taller plants with weaker stems (stem elongation).

Unlike air temperatures, root-zone temperatures need to be relatively stable.

Plants can be grouped according to their tolerance for cold temperatures:

  • cool season (“cold-tolerant”)
  • intermediate (“cold-temperate”)
  • warm season (“cold-sensitive”)

More about plant temperature

  • “Chapter 8: Physical Environmental Factors and Their Properties”, Plant Factory: An Indoor Vertical Farming System for Efficient Quality Food, edited by Toyoki Kozai, Genhua Niu, Michiko Takagaki
  • Christopher Currey, “Find your just-right temperature”, Oct 3, 2016, https://www.producegrower.com/article/hydroponic-production-primer-temperature/
  • Roberto Lopez, “Effects of Temperature on Greenhouse Crops”, Purdue University, http://www.e-gro.org/pdf/206.pdf

Of these, plants obtain carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and oxygen (O) freely from air (CO₂ and O₂) and water (H₂O).

The remaining nutrients are obtained from the soil (or alternative growing media) in the form of salts. This happens through multiple processes: by the root physically growing in contact with the nutrients (“root interception”), by dissolved nutrients flowing through the soil solution to the root (“mass flow”), and by dissolved nutrients diffusing through the soil solution to the depleted soil next to the plant root (“diffusion”).

Nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) are required in the largest amounts; commercial fertilizers are labeled with N-P-K ratios. Although nitrogen is abundant in the atmosphere (N₂), it is only available to plants in the form of ammonium (NH₄⁺, which has an acidic effect), nitrate (NO₃⁻, which has a basic effect), and urea.

Nitrogen is a key ingredient in many plant substances, including chlorophyll. It is used by leafy green crops (like lettuce) and more in the vegetative growth phase of fruiting crops. Phosphorus and especially potassium are more important for fruiting crops (such as tomatoes), as evidenced in the following diagram showing the macronutrient uptake across time for a tomato plant:

Electrical Conductivity (EC)

A EC meter measures electrical conductivity, which is an indicator of the amount of dissolved nutrients (mineral salts) in a solution.

  • EC cannot be used to determine the amounts or ratios of specific nutrients.
  • A Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) meter measures the amount of all kinds of dissolved solids (inorganic as well as organic) in a solution. Essentially it is an EC meter which performs an output conversion to TDS, measured in ppm. Be aware that the conversion factor varies across reference materials and nutrient suppliers in different applications and countries. For measuring hydroponic nutrients, the best approach is to use only EC, not TDS.

pH is the measure of acidity or alkalinity (basicity) of a solution, where acidic refers to having a high concentration of hydrogen ions (H⁺).

Soil pH is highly important as it affects the bioavailability of nutrients to plants.

  • An entry-level EC meter (e.g. ) costs 20–30 USD.
  • An entry-level pH meter (e.g. ) costs 50–60 USD; a professional-level pH meter (e.g. ) costs over 100 USD. You also need to buy liquid products for cleaning, storing (pH probes must be stored in a buffer solution), and calibrating the highly sensitive pH probe. These may be sold together as a kit. Be sure to get a pH meter with a replaceable probe. Even if unused, the pH electrode has a lifespan of only 6–18 months.
  • As an alternative to buying a pH meter, start with pH indicator drops, litmus paper, or even homemade red cabbage juice.

More about plant nutrition

  • UC Nursery and Floriculture Alliance, “English” playlist, https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGfKOdq24vnL-XPpMQGhfMdHbKOlb-BnO
  • Jeff Lowenfels, Teaming with Nutrients: The Organic Gardener’s Guide to Optimizing Plant Nutrition, 2013.
  • Mary M. Pratt, Practical Science for Gardeners, 2005.
  • Sonneveld and Voogt, Plant Nutrition for Greenhouse Crops.
  • “Chapter 11: Nutrition and Nutrient Uptake in Soilless Culture”, Plant Factory: An Indoor Vertical Farming System for Efficient Quality Food, edited by Toyoki Kozai, Genhua Niu, Michiko Takagaki
  • Khan Academy, “Acids, bases, and pH”, https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/water-acids-and-bases
  • Khan Academy, “Biogeochemical cycles”, https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/ecology#biogeochemical-cycles
  • NM State University, “Science of Agriculture: Cation Exchange”, https://scienceofagriculture.org/ch-cation.php

Soil is best understood from three perspectives simultaneously:

  • : Soil is a mixture of solids, liquids, and gases: typically 50% water, dissolved minerals, and various gases held in pores, 45% inorganic particles (sand, silt, and clay), and 5% organic matter (“soil organic matter”). is determined by the exact proportion of sand (most coarse), silt, and clay (most fine) particles.

Porosity refers to the percentage of pores (microsopic spaces) in the growing medium which can contain water or air. Different media have different water-holding capacity. For example, coarse-grained media (such as foam) has a low water-holding capacity (i.e. holds onto water weakly), medium-grained media (such as rockwool) has a medium water-holding capacity, and fine-grained media (such as peat) has a high water-holding capacity (i.e. holds onto water strongly). Water-holding capacity and air porosity should be chosen to be appropriate for the crop and container size.

  • : Soil is effective an aqueous solution containing dissolved minerals (nutrients) along with organic and inorganic particles. The particles commonly have negative charges, which attract nutrients with positive charges (cations). This allows the soil to hold and release certain nutrients. The holding capacity of a soil is called the cation-exchange capacity (CEC).

  • : Soil is an ecosystem of microbes, including bacteria and mycorrhizal fungi. See Jeff Lowenfels, Teaming with Microbes: The Organic Gardener’s Guide to The Soil Food Web and Teaming With Fungi: The Organic Grower’s Guide to Mycorrhizae

See overview table at https://github.com/CollapseLabs/gardening-for-engineers/blob/master/crops/dist/_crops.csv and individual pages at https://github.com/CollapseLabs/gardening-for-engineers/tree/master/crops/dist

The size and maturity values provided are for comparison purposes only. Actual values will vary considerably depending on seed variety, climate and other environmental factors, and growing technique.

Key here is to take an ecological (ecosystems) perspective.

refers to indoor farming in an urban context, scaling vertically, based on an early concept of farming in New York City skyscrapers. It implies the use of artifical lighting, either as a supplement or a replacement for sunlight. A vertical farm is also known by the Japanese term Plant Factory with Artificial Lighting (PFAL). Vertical farming may or may not involve vertical-plane growing (i.e. growing vertically in towers, as opposed to growing horizontally in racks).

Controlled-environment agriculture (CEA) refers to growing in a climate-controlled environment, typically a greenhouse but can also be completely indoors.

  • Kratky (passive) - best for leafy greens at small-scale
  • NFT - best for leafy greens at large-scale

items.title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
items.author: ayanb9440
items.content:
Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics.

1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with.

2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. You can train a detection model or define a ruleset once, but it will become obsolete in a matter of weeks as fraudsters figure out what your detection logic is. This means that you need a team regularly training models and updating rules based on new fraud patterns. Typically this takes a large data science/ML team. Kairos addresses this by introducing an MCP server, so that your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can define a decision workflow, train models on your data, and pick the variant that performs best.

An independent, AI-edited front page from Hacker News, regularly updated. Original reporting and images belong to the linked publishers. Not affiliated with The New York Times or Hacker News.

Current candidates use the first 90 official HN topstories API entries; first page means API ranks 1–30, and hnPage groups API ranks in thirties. Lead: selected separately by the balanced current-page lead policy. Other top stories remain current-first-page only and younger than seven days. Today desk previews and discussion placements are also younger than seven days. Logarithmic engagement (60 points / 25 comments; swapped for discussion) is multiplied by 2^(-ageDays), a 24-hour half-life with no additive freshness bonus. Independent sections contain up to 16 qualified stories in one ranked list across the sampled 30-day window, with no reserved older slots or seven-day section cutoff. Older stories can stay when their own meaningful engagement overcomes the stronger age penalty. Qualification requires 20 official HN points, 5 comments, or actual sampled current-page presence. Show fewer stories rather than weak filler. Fresh reposts compete using only their own submission age and counts; one normalized linked URL per edition. Permanent lead retirement is unchanged. Discovery is bounded, not exhaustive. The site reads accessible source pages; only relevant real images are used, without paywall bypasses.

Source snapshot: 2026-11-14 02:30 UTC. 253 verified candidates from current HN pages and a sampled 30-day search pool considered. Scores and comments reflect that snapshot.

items.title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
items.author: aarushyadav
items.content:
Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) (https://subvocal.company/). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech.

(Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.)

Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face:

We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology.

We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work:

- Signal changes due to sweat

- Electrical interference

- Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!!

So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text.

Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face:

Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place:

This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas.

That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data.

So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration).

We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well.

Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases.

For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at https://subvocal.co/preorder!

items.title: Show HN: OmniDiff – Opensource, super fast, content aware Git difftool, in Rust
items.author: FabCH
items.content:
I have been researching what the ultimate diff tool would look like, based on actual diffs in open source repositories.

OmniDiff can diff: code (25 languages), config, images, PDFs, archives, cursors, fonts...

It's fast. It can diff C++ files of tens of thousands of lines in under 100ms, on a 2023 ThinkPad T14s.

It's open source. AGPLv3.

It's based on real diffs. I looked at the 7400 repositories that are listed in Gentoo packages, sampled 2000 diffs and solved them manually to get a good understanding of what is needed, before putting together the diff pipelines for each content type. Incidentally, this also forms the basis of the CI pipeline, so the robustness of the codebase is quite high.

I'm still developing it. It's v0.3.0 at this time. But I have been using it daily as my git difftool for months now, and it works well.

AI Disclosure: Yes, I do use AI. No, I do not vibecode.

items.title: Show HN: A language model that lives in a boot sector
items.author: kerlenton
items.content:
All the ideas came from the boot sector demo scene where people had been writing chess and BASIC games in 512 bytes, even a C compiler. I wondered what one can do using a neural network instead of a program and generating boot logs for non-existent hardware was something fun to try.

Entire inference engine is 510 bytes of MBR, weights, vocab, and strings reside in the sectors following MBR. Small char-level neural network was trained on dmesg generated by machine, so machine produces Linux boot messages infinitely.

train.py performs precisely the same integer arithmetic operations as the asm code does and thus produces an output identical character-by-character to the one produced by QEMU. The difference analysis revealed my favorite bug. The characters at the beginning matched those generated by the simulator, but then the output diverged. I retrieved the hidden layer via QEMU’s debug port and compared the neurons' values with those of the simulator, one neuron at a time. Only the value of the first neuron was correct. The activation involves idiv, and idiv stores its remainder in edx. The pointer to the biases table was stored in edx, which resulted in the first neuron being biased correctly and the following ones using garbage. Now the bias' address is determined from the loop counter, and no pointers have to survive the division. Another bug I found simply by looking at the code before I did my first run-through: the BIOS print routine zeros out bx, but bx contains the predicted character number. This explains the push and pop of bx surrounding the print.

sectorllm is the most similar to my project, as it runs an actual 5-layer llama2 with attention mechanism in just 1.2K of assembly code. It is the trade-off in the opposite direction, as my engine needs to fit into one sector and therefore my network has just one hidden layer of int8 operations for dreaming the dmesg.

items.title: Show HN: I rebuilt my old canvas 3D library as a small WebGL 2 library – phoria2
items.author: kevs3d
items.content:
is a small, fast JavaScript library for 3D on the web - charts, labelled scenes, dashboards and product viewers, on a WebGL 2 renderer with an API you can learn in an afternoon. Designed for ease-of-use by agents and humans from the ground up!

  • PBR materials, instancing, points, lines, labels, picking, shadows, particles and glTF models.
  • No runtime dependencies, plain ES modules, and views that only draw when something changes.
  • Every option is validated, a mistake comes back as an error that details the fix - for you, or your coding agent.
  • MIT licensed. , then find the code, the docs and a React example on GitHub.

A rewrite of , a JavaScript library from 2013 that rendered 3D onto the canvas 2D context. Back when we were still wizards.
